q: The best single test for acute hepatitis A is:
Regarding hepatitis A, all are true EXCEPT:
A woman who is HBsAg-positive but HBeAg-negative delivers at term. The best management of the baby is:
o: Gamma globulin at birth and 1 month
HBIG only if cord blood is positive
HBIG and hepatitis B vaccine at birth, then routine doses
e: Infant of an HBsAg-positive mother: HBIG + birth-dose vaccine within 12–24 h.

q: A child has only anti-HBs positive. This means:
Chronic hepatitis B is most likely after infection:
e: About 90% of infants infected at birth become chronic.

q: An absolute contraindication to breastfeeding is:
o: Chronic hepatitis B in the mother
Acute hepatitis A in the mother
e: Hepatitis A, hepatitis B (after immunisation) and EBV do not contraindicate breastfeeding.

q: A 5-year-old with hepatitis is confused, bilirubin 16 mg/dl, INR 1.9, HBV and HCV negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
o: Acute liver failure from hepatitis A
e: Encephalopathy + INR ≥ 1.5 = acute liver failure; hepatitis A is the commonest cause.

q: The best guide to the severity of acute liver injury is:
e: INR rises within a day of synthetic failure.

q: A teenager with liver disease, tremor and falling school performance has low caeruloplasmin. Treatment is:
Laboratory evidence of decompensated chronic liver disease includes:
o: Low albumin and prolonged prothrombin time
e: Synthetic failure: low albumin, prolonged PT; enzymes may be near normal.

q: A child with varicella is given aspirin and develops vomiting and coma without jaundice. The diagnosis is:
e: Reye syndrome: encephalopathy + fatty liver, anicteric.

q: Hepatitis C in a 10-year-old is treated with:
e: WHO 2022: DAAs for all from 3 years.
